newsitem.title: USA: SMITHFIELD FOODS ENDS WASTEWATER DISCHARGES.
newsitem.headline: SMITHFIELD FOODS ENDS WASTEWATER DISCHARGES.

text.p: Smithfield Foods Inc said its wastewater discharges to the Pagan River ended Wednesday when its Smithfield Packing Co wastewater system was connected to the Hampton Roads Sanitation District's pipeline.
This connection was made more than 45 days ahead of schedule, the company said, noting Smithfield Foods had connected its Gwaltney facilities to the Hampton Roads, Va., system in June 1996.
By this action, Smithfield Foods said, the company has completed its obligations under a 1991 Consent Order issued by the Virginia State Water Control Board.

At that time, Smithfield Foods said, the company had the choice of upgrading its facilities or connecting to the sanitation district's system, which could not be extended to the Town of Smithfield without Smithfield Foods' commitment to use it. The Consent Order set compliance with the state's phosphorous standard and settled Smithfield Foods' court challenge to the reasonableness of that standard.
Richard N. Burton, who was Executive Director of the State Water Control Board in 1991, testified on behalf of Smithfield Foods in the recently-concluded federal trial in Norfolk.
This action was initiated by the federal complaint that the state's Consent Order did not bind its enforcement hand.

With Smithfield Foods' commitment, the company said, the sanitation district received needed financial help to upgrade and expand its Nansemond Wastewater Treatment Plant, which also needed to comply with the new phosphorus standard. The total cost of these facilities exceeds $65 million.
The sewer line to Smithfield was not completed until late March 1996. In June 1996, Smithfield Foods connected its Gwaltney facilities to the new pipeline.

The sanitation district did not give notice until June 25, 1997, that it could accept and treat the wastewater from the Smithfield Packing facilities. Excessive rain in 1996 and other factors had delayed the contractors' completion of the Nansemond Plant improvements.

Smithfield Foods said it has spent more than $2.7 million on new treatment units in the last two years, and will continue to run its existing facilities to pretreat its wastewaters before discharge to the sanitation district system. In addition, Smithfield Foods spent approximately $300,000 for a pump station to connect the Town of Smithfield's facilities to the pipeline.
Besides its pretreatment costs, Smithfield Foods said, it expects to pay more than $2 million per year for wastewater treatment.
